scenes.visual: Title card 'Why Reciprocal Crosses Split' over a large schematic family board. COLOUR MAP for both films: maternal chromosomes and organelles = TEAL; paternal chromosomes and allele tags = GOLD; white-eye allele = WHITE; red-eye allele = RED; Y chromosome and inactive marks = GREY. Flies are simple labelled cartoons, not anatomical drawings. The family board fills at least sixty percent of frame height.

scenes.tts: Why can swapping which parent has white eyes change every son? Morgan's reciprocal fly crosses looked almost identical at the start. Their offspring did not. The difference points to a chromosome route, not a new inheritance law.
scenes.caption: Why can swapping which parent has white eyes change every son? Morgan's reciprocal fly crosses looked almost identical at the start. Their offspring did not. The difference points to a chromosome route, not a new inheritance law.
scenes.visual: Two large parent pairs slide onto one carried family board. Pair A has a red-eyed mother and white-eyed father. Pair B swaps those eye colours. Question marks pulse over the empty offspring rows; label the whole drawing 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Why can swapping which parent has white eyes change every son? Morgan's reciprocal fly crosses looked almost identical at the start. Their offspring did not. The difference points to a chromosome route, not a new inheritance law.

scenes.tts: Start inside the flies. A female has a pair of X chromosomes. A male has an X and a Y. The white gene sits on the X, not the Y. Gene location decides which chromosome carries an allele through egg or sperm.
scenes.caption: Start inside the flies. A female has a pair of X chromosomes. A male has an X and a Y. The white gene sits on the X, not the Y. Gene location decides which chromosome carries an allele through egg or sperm.
scenes.visual: The parent cartoons enlarge into chromosome blocks. Two TEAL X blocks settle inside the mother. A GOLD X and GREY Y settle inside the father. A WHITE eye badge attaches to the relevant X; the Y shows no gene slot.
scenes.narration: Start inside the flies. A female has a pair of X chromosomes. A male has an X and a Y. The white gene sits on the X, not the Y. Gene location decides which chromosome carries an allele through egg or sperm.

scenes.tts: A male fly has one X, so he is hemizygous for white. His Y carries no white gene. A recessive white allele therefore shows in a male. No dominant allele can mask it. A female can carry white without showing it when a red allele is present.
scenes.caption: A male fly has one X, so he is hemizygous for white. His Y carries no white gene. A recessive white allele therefore shows in a male. No dominant allele can mask it. A female can carry white without showing it when a red allele is present.
scenes.visual: The male's single X expands beside the empty Y. A WHITE allele badge sends an arrow to a white eye. A ghosted second-X slot fades away while the label 'hemizygous: one allele present' appears.
scenes.narration: A male fly has one X, so he is hemizygous for white. His Y carries no white gene. A recessive white allele therefore shows in a male. No dominant allele can mask it. A female can carry white without showing it when a red allele is present.

scenes.tts: Now follow the chromosomes, not the eye colours. Sons receive their only X from their mother, while daughters receive their father's X. The father's Y makes the other route into sons. That unequal route is the key to the reciprocal-cross puzzle.
scenes.caption: Now follow the chromosomes, not the eye colours. Sons receive their only X from their mother, while daughters receive their father's X. The father's Y makes the other route into sons. That unequal route is the key to the reciprocal-cross puzzle.
scenes.visual: Return to the family board. TEAL maternal X blocks travel down into both daughter and son slots. GOLD paternal X blocks travel only into daughters. GREY Y blocks travel only into sons. The paths remain visible as broad coloured tracks.
scenes.narration: Now follow the chromosomes, not the eye colours. Sons receive their only X from their mother, while daughters receive their father's X. The father's Y makes the other route into sons. That unequal route is the key to the reciprocal-cross puzzle.

scenes.tts: Begin with a red-eyed mother carrying only red alleles. Every child receives her red X. The white-eyed father's X reaches daughters, where her red allele masks it. Every offspring is red-eyed. The daughters carry white, but their red maternal allele determines eye colour.
scenes.caption: Begin with a red-eyed mother carrying only red alleles. Every child receives her red X. The white-eyed father's X reaches daughters, where her red allele masks it. Every offspring is red-eyed. The daughters carry white, but their red maternal allele determines eye colour.
scenes.visual: On Pair A, RED badges ride the maternal X tracks into every offspring. The father's WHITE badge rides only into daughters, then sits behind a RED badge. All offspring eye icons turn RED together.
scenes.narration: Begin with a red-eyed mother carrying only red alleles. Every child receives her red X. The white-eyed father's X reaches daughters, where her red allele masks it. Every offspring is red-eyed. The daughters carry white, but their red maternal allele determines eye colour.

scenes.tts: Reverse only the parental eye colours. The mother now carries white alleles, and the father carries red. Before the chromosomes move, which offspring will have white eyes?
scenes.caption: Reverse only the parental eye colours. The mother now carries white alleles, and the father carries red. Before the chromosomes move, which offspring will have white eyes?
scenes.visual: Pair A smoothly transforms into Pair B without changing positions. WHITE badges settle on both maternal X blocks; a RED badge settles on the paternal X. Offspring slots return to neutral. A question card reads 'Which offspring are white-eyed?'
scenes.narration: Reverse only the parental eye colours. The mother now carries white alleles, and the father carries red. Before the chromosomes move, which offspring will have white eyes?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Keep the reciprocal parents and question visible. A quiet ring timer completes one turn while chromosome blocks drift subtly in place.

scenes.tts: Every daughter gets the father's red X and a maternal white X. She is red-eyed. Every son gets a maternal white X and the father's Y. He is white-eyed. This is criss-cross inheritance: father to daughter, mother to son.
scenes.caption: Every daughter gets the father's red X and a maternal white X. She is red-eyed. Every son gets a maternal white X and the father's Y. He is white-eyed. This is criss-cross inheritance: father to daughter, mother to son.
scenes.visual: The stored tracks animate. GOLD paternal X blocks with RED badges enter daughters. TEAL maternal X blocks with WHITE badges enter all offspring. GREY Y blocks enter sons. Daughter eyes turn RED; son eyes turn WHITE.
scenes.narration: Every daughter gets the father's red X and a maternal white X. She is red-eyed. Every son gets a maternal white X and the father's Y. He is white-eyed. This is criss-cross inheritance: father to daughter, mother to son.

scenes.tts: The two crosses use the same red and white alleles. Only the carrier's sex changed. Yet their first offspring differ. Reciprocal crosses can separate X-linked inheritance from ordinary autosomal inheritance. An ordinary autosomal allele would not change routes when the carrier's sex changes.
scenes.caption: The two crosses use the same red and white alleles. Only the carrier's sex changed. Yet their first offspring differ. Reciprocal crosses can separate X-linked inheritance from ordinary autosomal inheritance. An ordinary autosomal allele would not change routes when the carrier's sex changes.
scenes.visual: Both completed family boards align side by side. Matching allele badges glow, then the parental-sex labels swap. A bracket highlights the different son rows. An autosomal block beside them sends one copy from each parent to every offspring and yields matching rows.
scenes.narration: The two crosses use the same red and white alleles. Only the carrier's sex changed. Yet their first offspring differ. Reciprocal crosses can separate X-linked inheritance from ordinary autosomal inheritance. An ordinary autosomal allele would not change routes when the carrier's sex changes.

scenes.tts: This pattern does not replace Mendel's segregation. It adds chromosome location to the bookkeeping. Inheritance patterns depend on allele identity, chromosome location, and parental origin. Here, location changes the route. Parent of origin matters here because sex determines the chromosome route.
scenes.caption: This pattern does not replace Mendel's segregation. It adds chromosome location to the bookkeeping. Inheritance patterns depend on allele identity, chromosome location, and parental origin. Here, location changes the route. Parent of origin matters here because sex determines the chromosome route.
scenes.visual: The two X tracks compress into a three-part ledger: 'allele identity', 'chromosome location', 'parental origin'. All three entries glow, 'chromosome location' brightest, with a small link from 'parental origin' labelled 'via the parent's sex'. A small label reads 'ordinary segregation continues'.
scenes.narration: This pattern does not replace Mendel's segregation. It adds chromosome location to the bookkeeping. Inheritance patterns depend on allele identity, chromosome location, and parental origin. Here, location changes the route. Parent of origin matters here because sex determines the chromosome route.

scenes.tts: Read the family board from the son backward. His X points to his mother. Read a daughter backward, and one X points to each parent. Swapping the carrier therefore changes where the allele can go. The allele itself behaves the same; its possible destinations have changed.
scenes.caption: Read the family board from the son backward. His X points to his mother. Read a daughter backward, and one X points to each parent. Swapping the carrier therefore changes where the allele can go. The allele itself behaves the same; its possible destinations have changed.
scenes.visual: A spotlight moves from a son backward along the TEAL X track to the mother. It then moves from a daughter backward along TEAL and GOLD tracks to both parents. The tracks fold into a single X-shaped route map.
scenes.narration: Read the family board from the son backward. His X points to his mother. Read a daughter backward, and one X points to each parent. Swapping the carrier therefore changes where the allele can go. The allele itself behaves the same; its possible destinations have changed.

scenes.visual: End card with one line only: 'The route of an X-linked allele depends on its carrier parent.'
